title: Insurance records and maritime risk
bodyMd:
In an invented study of an eighteenth-century port, historians discover that the surviving insurance ledgers list relatively few voyages to a nearby coast known from other records to have been commercially important. One interpretation is that merchants regarded those voyages as unusually safe and therefore did not insure them. That interpretation treats the ledger as a neutral record of opportunities to purchase insurance.

The historians propose another possibility. Several large trading families maintained reciprocal arrangements under which participants covered one another’s losses. Such arrangements could substitute for a formal policy, but were recorded in family correspondence rather than in the ledgers of specialist insurers. A voyage’s absence from the insurance ledger could thus reflect the institution used to manage risk, rather than the amount of risk merchants perceived. Correspondence describing joint compensation after a storm supports the existence of the alternative arrangement, although it does not reveal how every uninsured voyage was financed.

This institutional explanation also changes how the price of a formal policy should be interpreted. If merchants chose between reciprocal arrangements and specialist insurers, the voyages appearing in formal ledgers might be a selected subset. For example, merchants excluded from family networks could have relied more heavily on formal insurance even when their routes resembled those of network members. A comparison of premiums across ports would then need information about who could use each institution, not merely about distance and weather. The historians do not claim that maritime hazards were irrelevant to premiums. They argue that hazard and institutional access can jointly shape the records that later scholars observe.
